title: THEY PREACHED IN GOD’S NAME… WHILE SLEEPING WITH THEIR NEIGHBORS’ WIVES. THEN GOD EXPOSED THEM.
paragraphs: THEY PREACHED IN GOD’S NAME… WHILE SLEEPING WITH THEIR NEIGHBORS’ WIVES. THEN GOD EXPOSED THEM.

Two false prophets. Two hidden scandals. One terrifying declaration from God. Jeremiah 29:21–23 reveals what happens when people use the name of the Lord to conceal the very sins He calls them to repent of—and why the only hope for any sinner is the grace and truth found in Jesus Christ.
They probably never imagined their names would be remembered for this.
Not for their sermons.
Not for their spiritual influence.
Not for the comforting words they spoke to people desperate for hope.
But for the sins they committed when they thought nobody important was watching.
Imagine sitting among the exiles in Babylon, listening to a man who claims to speak for God.
He sounds confident. He speaks with authority. He knows the language of faith. He tells frightened families what they desperately want to hear.
And perhaps you believe him.
Why wouldn't you?
He speaks in the name of the Lord.
But somewhere behind that religious confidence, another story is unfolding.
A married woman. A violated covenant. A neighbor betrayed. A secret that was never secret to God.
And then a letter arrives from Jerusalem.
A letter carrying a message that will outlive kingdoms.
God names the men.
God names the sin.
And suddenly, the very people who claimed to speak for heaven are standing exposed before heaven's judgment.
Their names were Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah.
And their story is recorded in Jeremiah 29:21–23.
But before you decide this is merely another account of corrupt religious leaders, there is something you need to understand.
The most dangerous part of this story is not that two men were caught in adultery. It is that they were using God's name while living in rebellion against His Word.
And if we read this passage only to condemn them, without allowing Scripture to examine our own hearts, we may miss the warning entirely.
Because the distance between a public profession of faith and a private life of compromise can become terrifyingly small.
Jeremiah was writing during one of the darkest chapters of Judah's history.
Jerusalem was under Babylonian domination. Many of God's people had been taken from their homeland. Families were grieving. Their familiar world had collapsed.
They were desperate for reassurance.
And desperate people can become vulnerable to voices promising relief without repentance, restoration without waiting, and divine blessing without submission to divine truth.
Into that painful situation came prophets claiming that God had sent them.
But God had not.
Listen carefully to what the Lord declared through Jeremiah:

"Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes." — Jeremiah 29:21, KJV
Notice the accusation.
They were not merely mistaken about a prediction.
They were prophesying lies in God's name.
That changes everything.
They were attaching divine authority to messages God had not given them.
They were placing the reputation of the Holy One behind their own words.
And when the Lord revealed what else they had done, the scandal became even more disturbing.

"Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the LORD." — Jeremiah 29:23, KJV
Read those final words again.
"Even I know, and am a witness."
There are moments in Scripture when the weight of a sentence is greater than an entire sermon.
This is one of them.
The Hebrew text concludes with:
וְאָנֹכִי הַיּוֹדֵעַ וָעֵד נְאֻם־יְהוָה
Ve'anokhi hayyodea va'ed, ne'um-Adonai.
A careful rendering is:
"And I am the One who knows, and a witness, declares the LORD."
The Hebrew divine name appears in the biblical text; Adonai is the traditional spoken substitute used here in transliteration.
The statement is devastating because it removes every imagined hiding place.
God knows.
God witnesses.
God does not need another person to discover what He has already seen.
The passage also uses the Hebrew word נְבָלָה (nevalah), rendered "villany" in the King James Version. It describes disgraceful, morally outrageous conduct—not simply an embarrassing mistake.
Their adultery was not treated as a minor personal weakness.
It was a serious violation of God's moral law and of the marriage covenants they had dishonored.
And their false prophecies were not harmless religious enthusiasm.
They were lies spoken under the authority of a God who had never commanded them.
Two forms of betrayal.
One against their neighbors and their wives.
Another against the truth of God.
And both committed by men who claimed spiritual authority.
Can you imagine the devastation left behind?
The husband who trusted his neighbor.
The wife whose marriage was violated.
The families who had listened to these men speak about God.
The ordinary believers who may have wondered whether anything they had been taught could still be trusted.
Scripture does not tell us the personal reactions of these families, so we should not invent their stories as facts.
But anyone who has experienced betrayal knows that sin rarely stops hurting at the boundary of the person committing it.
It spreads.
Through marriages.
Through friendships.
Through families.
Through communities.
And when religious authority is involved, it can leave wounded people struggling to separate the character of God from the conduct of those who claimed to represent Him.
Perhaps that is why this passage feels painfully relevant even thousands of years later.
Because some people know what it means to discover that someone they trusted spiritually was living a completely different life behind closed doors.
Some have watched a respected leader fall.
Some have been manipulated by religious language.
Some have experienced betrayal from someone who could quote Scripture beautifully but refused to obey it privately.
And some are carrying wounds that became even harder to heal because the person who caused them claimed to be serving God.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
The hypocrisy of a person who speaks about Jesus is not proof that Jesus is a hypocrite.
The betrayal of a religious leader does not change the holiness of Christ.
The failure of a preacher does not make the Gospel false.
Jesus never asked you to build your salvation upon the moral perfection of another sinner.
He calls you to trust Him.
The One who is faithful when human beings are not.
The One who speaks truth even when truth is costly.
The One who never uses the vulnerable for His own gratification.
But there is another side of this passage that we must not avoid.
It is possible to be outraged by the sins of Ahab and Zedekiah while remaining strangely comfortable with our own hidden compromises.
We read about adultery and immediately think of somebody else's marriage.
We read about false prophecy and immediately remember somebody else's ministry.
We read about hypocrisy and immediately picture somebody else's face.
Yet Jesus does not allow us to keep every warning at a comfortable distance.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches that adultery is not only a matter of outward behavior; lustful intent also reveals the condition of the heart.
He exposes the inner life.
Not because every sinful thought is identical in its consequences to the physical act of adultery, but because sin begins deeper than the actions other people can see.
And suddenly, the question becomes personal.
What am I hiding?
What have I excused because nobody has confronted me?
Where have I learned to sound spiritually mature while refusing to surrender something God has already condemned?
Maybe it is a conversation you know should have ended.
Maybe it is an emotional attachment you keep calling harmless.
Maybe it is a secret habit you have repeatedly promised God you would abandon.
Maybe it is bitterness you have carefully disguised as discernment.
Maybe it is the need to appear holy while privately refusing correction.
Not every struggle is the same. Not every temptation means someone has committed the same offense as these false prophets.
But every believer needs the humility to ask whether there is a difference between the faith they profess and the life they are actually living.
Because a Christian can become very skilled at defending a reputation while neglecting the condition of the soul.
You can know the right worship songs.
You can post Bible verses.
You can defend sound doctrine.
You can attend church every week.
You can even serve in ministry.
And still have an area of your life where you are resisting the Lord who saved you.
That is not a reason to abandon the church or despair of God's mercy.
It is a reason to stop pretending.
There is a difference between a believer struggling against sin and a person deliberately protecting sin while claiming God's approval.
The struggling believer needs encouragement, truth, accountability, and grace.
The person defending rebellion needs to hear God's warning.
And both need Jesus.
Here is where Jeremiah's account becomes even more sobering.
God did not merely announce that these prophets had sinned.
He announced judgment.
Jeremiah 29:22 says their fate would become so notorious among the exiles that their names would be used in a curse.
The text says Nebuchadnezzar would roast them in the fire.
That is a severe historical judgment announced against these particular men. Scripture does not authorize us to predict that every false teacher or adulterer will suffer the same earthly punishment.
Nor should we take pleasure in the violence of their fate.
The point is not to enjoy another person's destruction.
The point is to understand that God takes evil seriously—even when it is committed by people who speak His name.
And this raises a question that should disturb every person who has ever been tempted to use religion as a hiding place.
What happens when God refuses to protect the image we have constructed?
What happens when the truth we have avoided finally reaches the light?
For Ahab and Zedekiah, the prophetic announcement was judgment.
But the Bible does not end with Jeremiah 29.
And the story of God's dealings with sinners does not end with exposure.
Centuries later, another scene unfolds.
This time, Jesus is standing before people who have brought Him a woman accused of adultery.
John 8:3–11 describes a confrontation in which the woman's accusers seek to use her case to test Jesus.
Jesus does not declare adultery acceptable.
He does not redefine sin to make the crowd comfortable.
But neither does He allow the accusers to turn the woman into a convenient instrument for their own purposes.
After the accusers depart, He tells her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV
Do not miss the beauty of those two movements.
Mercy.
And a command to leave sin behind.
Grace does not mean sin was never serious.
Grace means that sinners can encounter the mercy of Christ without being told that their rebellion is harmless.
And we must handle this comparison carefully.

The woman in John 8 is not Ahab or Zedekiah. The circumstances are different, and the passage does not tell us the details of her life afterward. The account also has a well-known textual history: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest Greek manuscripts, a fact many modern Bibles acknowledge.
Nevertheless, the mercy and holiness displayed in this traditional account agree with truths clearly taught elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Jesus calls people to turn away from sin.
Jesus offers forgiveness that no human being can manufacture.
And His mercy is never permission to continue harming others.
This is the Gospel's astonishing tension.
God is more holy than we dare imagine.
And in Jesus Christ, His grace reaches sinners more deeply than they could ever deserve.
The apostle Paul writes:
All.
Not merely false prophets.
Not merely adulterers.
Not merely the people whose scandals became public.
All.
That includes the preacher.
The congregation.
The wounded.
The respected.
The ashamed.
The person reading this article who has never told anyone what they did.
But Paul does not stop there.
Romans 3:24 speaks of believers being justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace or favor.
And ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis) means redemption or release secured through a ransom.
These words are not decorative religious language.
They point to what God has accomplished through Christ.
Forgiveness is not something we purchase by becoming impressive enough.
Redemption is not something we earn by hiding our worst moments successfully.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
His cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of God.
At Calvary, grace was not cheap.
It was purchased at the cost of the Savior's life.
And because He lives, repentance does not have to end in hopelessness.
Maybe your story contains a scandal.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by choices you deeply regret.
Maybe you have lied to protect your image.
Maybe you have walked away from God because someone claiming to represent Him hurt you.
Maybe you are not the person who committed the betrayal.
Maybe you are the one who has spent years trying to recover from it.
The Gospel does not demand that you pretend the damage never happened.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Repentance does not erase consequences.
And reconciliation cannot be forced upon a wounded person simply because the offender says they are sorry.
Real repentance involves turning away from sin, speaking truth, accepting responsibility, and seeking to make things right where possible.
Where there has been exploitation, abuse, or coercion, protecting those harmed and pursuing appropriate accountability matters.
Grace is not a cover for continued wrongdoing.
But neither is your worst chapter necessarily the final chapter of your life.
Listen to the promise of 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
The Greek verb translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from homologeō, meaning to confess or acknowledge.
Confession is not the art of explaining why our sin was understandable.
It is agreeing with the truth about what we have done.
No disguise.
No spiritual performance.
No blaming everybody else.
Just a sinner coming into the light before a merciful God.
And perhaps the hardest prayer you will ever pray is also one of the most liberating:

"Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have defended what You have called sin. I have been more concerned about what people think of me than about obeying You. Have mercy on me. Teach me to walk in truth. Change what I cannot change by my own strength."
There is no magic in repeating those words.
But there is real hope in turning to the living Christ with genuine faith and repentance.
And if you have already confessed your sins and are struggling under crushing shame, remember this:
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The enemy of your soul would love to convince you that exposure means your life is over.
The Gospel tells a different story.
Sin must be brought into the light.
But the light of Christ is not only a place where evil is revealed.
It is where sinners may find cleansing, truth, and a new way to live.
Ahab and Zedekiah remind us of the danger of claiming divine authority while rejecting divine truth.
Jesus shows us the only Savior who can redeem those who come to Him.
And that brings us to a question far more important than whether you were shocked by the scandal.
What will you do with the truth God has placed before you today?
Will you simply share another story about the sins of religious leaders?
Or will you allow the Word of God to examine your own heart?
Will you keep defending the habit that is slowly destroying your peace?
Will you keep postponing the apology you know you owe?
Will you keep mistaking public admiration for spiritual maturity?
Or will you finally come to Jesus without the mask?
Perhaps someone reading this is trembling because the words have reached a place they have kept hidden for years.
If that is you, you do not have to publish your private sins in a comment section to prove your repentance.
You can seek the Lord honestly, and when necessary, reach out to a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian, counselor, or appropriate authority for help and accountability.
And if you have witnessed the mercy of Christ restoring what sin once damaged, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness without exposing another person's private life.
Somebody reading those words may realize they are not alone.
Somebody may find the courage to seek help.
Somebody may finally understand that Jesus is not finished calling sinners to repentance and offering them grace.
That is why this message deserves to travel beyond this page.
Not because scandals attract attention.
Not because another person's failure makes entertaining content.
But because the truth of God's Word can reach someone who has been living between secret shame and desperate hope.
Sometimes the first step toward spiritual renewal begins with hearing one passage of Scripture explained with compassion and truth.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ, there is another meaningful way to help this ministry continue.
It does not purchase forgiveness, guarantee blessing, or make you more righteous before the Lord.
Jesus has already accomplished what money could never buy.
For believers who choose to include Gospel Warrior in their regular Christian giving, that support can be a genuine expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
The Bible teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
What matters is that generosity flows from sincere love for God and neighbor.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
It is helping biblical teaching reach the discouraged believer, the person questioning faith, the Christian seeking spiritual maturity, and the soul longing to understand the grace of Jesus Christ.
These free resources are part of the heart behind the ministry: making Christian teaching and spiritual nourishment more accessible, not putting the Gospel behind a paywall.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite people to study Scripture.
Encourage someone to seek Christ.
A simple act of sharing may place biblical truth before someone who would never have searched for it on their own.
Our mission is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people back to Jesus.
Back to His Word.
Back to the cross.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the Savior who alone has the power to make sinners new.
And now, before you leave, remember the two names that began this story.
Ahab.
Zedekiah.
Men who spoke in God's name while betraying His commands.
Their names remain in Scripture as a warning.
Not because God wanted His people to become obsessed with scandal, but because truth matters, holiness matters, and no claim to spiritual authority places anyone beyond accountability.
Yet there is another name greater than theirs.
A name above every name.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never lied in the Father's name.
The One who never betrayed His calling.
The One who was tempted yet without sin.
The One who bore our sins on the cross and rose victorious from the grave.
The One who can forgive the guilty without calling evil good.
The One who can comfort the wounded without minimizing what happened to them.
The One who can take a life fractured by sin and begin the patient, holy work of restoration.
So do not finish this article merely asking, "How could those two prophets do something so terrible?"
Ask something deeper.
"Lord, is there anything in my life that I am still afraid to surrender to You?"
And when He brings the truth into the light, do not run farther into darkness.
Run to Christ.
Because the God who knows every hidden thing is also the God who, through Jesus Christ, calls repentant sinners out of hiding and into the freedom of His grace.
The secret you are terrified to bring into the light may be the very place where your surrender to Jesus finally begins.
